VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository includes dataset loading and preprocessing code, but there is no explicit validation or evidence ensuring that the data has no all-black images, no unexpected characters in text, or that tables/features are checked for reasonableness. Without running the code and inspecting the resulting data, I cannot confirm these conditions. The code relies primarily on standard datasets and basic transforms, which is common, but does not implement or log data-quality checks that would directly satisfy the test case.
EVIDENCE:
- MNIST loading uses torchvision with ToTensor only; no checks for image content or anomalies are present [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:208-229].
- CIFAR10 loading similarly uses ToTensor only; no additional validation is performed [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:251-272].
- CIFAR train/eval transforms perform random flip/crop and normalization; there are no safeguards against all-black or corrupted images [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/transform.py:18-28] and [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/transform.py:41-50].

- QM9Energy dataset is read from HDF5 and wrapped as torch_geometric Data objects without checks for NaNs, ranges, or outliers in feature values [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:647-690].

Additional information needed to make a determination:
- Run logs or metrics from data validation steps (if any) confirming no all-black images, no unexpected characters in text, and reasonable feature distributions.
- Sample dumps or summaries (e.g., histograms, min/max, NaN counts) of the loaded datasets produced by executing the data loading pipeline.
- Any unit/integration tests or scripts in the project that perform data-quality checks and their results.

tests.description:
VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository defines separate train-time and eval-time transforms where only the train transform contains random augmentations, and the eval transform is deterministic. However, the code that wires these transforms into the actual data loaders (via mlwiz’s DataProvider and external configuration files) is not included, so we cannot verify that the validation and test datasets indeed use only the deterministic preprocessing in practice.
EVIDENCE: 
- The repository defines distinct CIFAR transforms: train includes random augmentations while eval is deterministic: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/transform.py:17-28] shows RandomHorizontalFlip and RandomCrop; [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/transform.py:41-50] shows only Normalize.
- Dataset classes accept transform_train and transform_eval but their application is handled outside this code (by mlwiz DataProvider). For example, NCI1 stores self.transform_train and self.transform_eval in its constructor, implying intended separate transforms: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:292-304].
- The Multi30K dataset explicitly states runtime preprocessing is handled by DataProvider (external to this repo): [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:527-528].
- The README references external config files (DATA_CONFIGS and EXP_CONFIGS) not present here, which likely specify and wire the transforms for train/val/test splits: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/README.md:5-11].
- Offline processing for MNIST/CIFAR uses ToTensor deterministically for both train and test, but this does not demonstrate the runtime augmentations are constrained to training only: MNIST train/test transforms are deterministic ToTensor only: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:212-217,218-227]; CIFAR10 train/test offline transforms are also only ToTensor: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dataset.py:255-259,261-270].

Additional information needed: The mlwiz DataProvider configuration or code that instantiates dataset_getter with transform_train for training and transform_eval for validation/test (e.g., DATA_CONFIGS/EXP_CONFIGS or the relevant mlwiz code snippet) or run logs confirming which transforms are applied to each split. Without these, we cannot conclusively determine that augmentations are only applied to the training dataset and that val/test use deterministic preprocessing in this setup.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The codebase contains forward paths that create CPU tensors and combine them with potentially GPU-resident tensors without moving them to a common device, violating the requirement of consistent device handling and risking implicit or erroneous CPU<->GPU transfers. Dtype handling is also inconsistent, mixing explicit float32 with torch.get_default_dtype in different places.
EVIDENCE: 
- In the MLP forward, a CPU tensor is created inside the forward pass and used in arithmetic with h, which will be on whatever device the input is on. If h is on GPU, this causes a device mismatch or implicit transfer: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/model.py:97-104]. Specifically, line 101: h = h / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor([self.num_hidden_neurons])) creates a CPU tensor without device, then divides a potentially GPU tensor by it.
- Static CPU tensors used as class attributes for GMNNQM9Energy (scale and shift) are not registered as buffers or moved explicitly; if the model/data are moved to GPU, these remain on CPU unless ScaleShiftLayer handles it internally (not shown in this repo): [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/model.py:196-203]. Similarly in the dynamic variant: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dynamic_architecture.py:918-925].
- Contrast with dynamic architecture code that correctly places rescaling tensors on the same device as activations (indicating awareness but inconsistent application across the repo): [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dynamic_architecture.py:879-886] and [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dynamic_architecture.py:121-127].
- Mixed dtype policy usage: some places rely on torch.get_default_dtype(), others hardcode dtype=torch.float32 (e.g., rescaling constant), indicating inconsistent dtype handling: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dynamic_architecture.py:531-536] vs. many calls using torch.get_default_dtype() across distributions (e.g., [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/distribution.py:101-116], [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/distribution.py:310-321]).

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The evaluation phase can mutate the model’s architecture using randomness (without retraining) due to adaptive-width updates performed inside the forward pass. This introduces non-determinism in evaluation accuracy across runs.
EVIDENCE: 
- The AWN model’s forward pass unconditionally updates the network width via update_width() unless skip_update is set, with no check for training vs. evaluation mode: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/model.py:777-799].
- update_width() calls change_shape() on the dynamic architecture for each layer to match a computed truncation number (based on the learned distribution), regardless of mode: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/model.py:718-733].
- When increasing width, change_shape() randomly initializes the newly added neurons using a standard Gaussian via normal_ for both weights and biases, consuming the global RNG without any seed control: [/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/dynamic_architecture.py:313-336].
- Because these random initializations are performed during forward() (i.e., during evaluation as well), running evaluation multiple times from the same trained weights can produce different architectures/parameters on first forward per run, leading to different accuracy values across runs even without retraining.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository uses explicit Python loops to perform operations over model parameters that could be implemented more efficiently with vectorized tensor operations.
EVIDENCE: In the AWN model forward pass, the Gaussian prior term over parameters is computed using a Python list comprehension iterating over each parameter tensor in a layer and summing elementwise squares. This can be replaced by a single vectorized operation by flattening and concatenating parameters (e.g., torch.nn.utils.parameters_to_vector) and computing the squared norm in one shot, avoiding Python-level iteration.
- The looped computation (per layer): [
/workspace/Adaptive Width Neural Networks [p6Ek7Qg577]/supplementary/AWNN_suppl/model.py:840-845]
  log_p_theta = sum(
      [
          -(p**2).sum() / 2 / (self.theta_prior_scale**2)
          for p in layer.parameters()
      ]
  )
This explicit loop over tensors is a candidate for vectorization (e.g., parameters_to_vector(layer.parameters()) to build a single vector and compute -(vec.pow(2).sum()) / (2 * self.theta_prior_scale.pow(2)) directly) and thus violates the test condition prohibiting explicit control flow where matrix operations could be used more efficiently.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains code that does not consistently place the model and inputs on the same device. In particular, one LLM implementation loads a Hugging Face model with device_map='auto' and then unconditionally moves inputs to 'cuda', which can lead to device mismatches or implicit transfers if the model or parts of it reside on a different device. There are also other components that hardcode device='cuda' without checks. While some modules handle device and dtype properly, the presence of these inconsistent patterns means the repo does not satisfy the test case.
EVIDENCE:
- In the TDW module’s LLM, the model is created with device_map='auto' and 4-bit quantization, but inputs are forced to CUDA:
  [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/tdw_mat/Ours_LLM/LLM.py:121-126]
  [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/tdw_mat/Ours_LLM/LLM.py:228-231]
  - Line 125 shows: self.hf_model = LlamaForCausalLM.from_pretrained(self.lm_id, device_map='auto', load_in_4bit=True)
  - Line 228 shows: input_ids = self.hf_tokenizer(flat, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to('cuda')
  This forces inputs to CUDA regardless of where the model is actually placed by device_map='auto', violating consistent device placement.
- The TDW detection pipeline hardcodes device='cuda' for the MMDetection inferencer without availability checks or alignment with input tensors:
  [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/tdw_mat/tdw-gym/detection.py:8-18]
  - Lines 11-16: self.inferencer = DetInferencer(..., device = "cuda")
- By contrast, the CWAH LLM correctly ensures inputs follow the model’s device and applies a dtype policy, indicating mixed practices:
  [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/LLM/LLM.py:145-157]
  [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/LLM/LLM.py:216-221]
  - Lines 145-149: device_map="auto" and torch_dtype="auto" for Qwen; Lines 152-157: pipeline with torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 and device_map="auto" for LLaMA.
  - Line 216: tokenizer(...).to(model.device) moves inputs to the model’s device explicitly.
These inconsistencies across the repository fail the criterion that model and inputs are consistently moved to one device with a consistent dtype policy and no implicit CPU<->GPU transfers.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The evaluation pipeline contains multiple uncontrolled sources of randomness (Unity environment behavior and LLM action selection) without consistently fixing seeds, so repeated evaluations can yield different success/accuracy values even without retraining.
EVIDENCE: 
- Unity environment injects randomness during execution: in step(), when the agent is deemed stuck, it randomly redirects the agent using NumPy’s global RNG (no seed fixed in the test scripts), which changes episode outcomes across runs: [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/envs/unity_environment.py:426-433].
- The UnityEnvironment constructor also uses a random base port by default (though often overridden), indicating additional non-deterministic behavior via NumPy if defaults are used: [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/envs/unity_environment.py:21-30].
- Test scripts seed only Python’s random, not NumPy’s RNG. For example, test_symbolic_LLM.py sets random.seed(id_run) but does not set np.random.seed, so the Unity environment’s NumPy-based randomness remains uncontrolled: [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/testing_agents/test_symbolic_LLM.py:1-25].
- LLM action selection contains additional stochastic behavior:
  - If the model’s output cannot be parsed, it falls back to a random action: [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/LLM/LLM.py:345-356].
  - Optional random reasoning logic uses random.random (unseeded at evaluation level unless explicitly controlled), further introducing non-determinism: [/workspace/From Assumptions to Actions_ Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents [GODFBZhFcX]/supplementary/PCE/cwah/LLM/LLM.py:844-846].
- Although arguments default to temperature=0 for LLM calls, the Unity environment’s NumPy randomness alone is sufficient to invalidate determinism of evaluation outcomes (no np.random.seed set in test scripts).

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository primarily orchestrates multi-agent LLM debate workflows and string-based data processing. Where batching could improve efficiency (e.g., sequence generation), the code uses batched/tokenized tensor operations through Transformers instead of per-example Python loops. There are no evident cases where numeric array/tensor computations are implemented with explicit Python control flow that should be vectorized; loops present are for orchestration, I/O, or textual parsing, not matrix-style computation.
EVIDENCE: 
- Batched generation uses vectorized tokenizer/model calls rather than per-example loops:
  - Batch encode prompts with tokenizer.batch_encode_plus, returning tensors suitable for single batched forward passes [/workspace/Internalizing Self-Consistency in Language Models_ Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment [Ma0LTdFVeL]/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/model.py:589-607].
  - Move the entire batch to device and proceed as a batch [/workspace/Internalizing Self-Consistency in Language Models_ Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment [Ma0LTdFVeL]/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/model.py:609-614].
- The debate pipeline calls the batched generation routine for all contexts of a given agent, avoiding a loop of single-item forward passes [/workspace/Internalizing Self-Consistency in Language Models_ Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment [Ma0LTdFVeL]/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/debate.py:591-593].
- Statistical summaries are computed with NumPy reductions (mean/std) rather than manual summation in loops; the loops in this section collect/parse string answers, not numeric arrays that would benefit from vectorization [/workspace/Internalizing Self-Consistency in Language Models_ Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment [Ma0LTdFVeL]/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/utils.py:354-365].
- Majority vote logic and other control flows iterate over text/string answers to determine consensus; these are not matrix-amenable operations (no missed vectorization opportunity) [/workspace/Internalizing Self-Consistency in Language Models_ Multi-Agent Consensus Alignment [Ma0LTdFVeL]/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/debate.py:94-108].

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The evaluation pipeline uses stochastic text generation (sampling) during debate/evaluation, and in the default (scheduled) evaluation path there is no seeding to ensure reproducibility. Therefore, running the model evaluation multiple times without retraining can yield different outputs and thus different accuracy values.
EVIDENCE:
- Default generation uses sampling: temperature defaults to 1 (non-greedy), enabling stochastic sampling.
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/args.py:51-55 ]
- In the model-based (distributed) generation path, sampling is enabled when temperature != 0, i.e., do_sample=True. 
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/model.py:628-637 ]
- The default configuration enables the scheduler and adapter mode for evaluation, steering the code to the scheduled path by default.
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/args.py:189-214 ]
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/orchestrator.py:302-325 ]
- In the scheduled evaluation path, batch generation always sets do_sample=True and there is no call to set any random seed for reproducibility.
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/scheduler.py:500-511 ]
  (No seeding in scheduler: no set_random_seed invocation anywhere in this file.)
- While the distributed path seeds randomness inside Agent initialization:
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/model.py:288-294 ]
  [ /workspace/repo_clean/supplementary/maca_anonymous_submission/utils.py:107-120 ]
  the default scheduled path bypasses Agent for generation and does not seed, leaving sampling nondeterministic.

Given the above, evaluation accuracy is not guaranteed to be deterministic across runs without retraining, especially in the default scheduled mode where sampling is enabled and unseeded.

VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository clearly implements a data loading and preprocessing pipeline for graph datasets (not images or text), but without executing the code or inspecting the actual datasets/outputs, it is not possible to verify that the loaded data are free of anomalies and that feature values are “reasonable.” The test’s examples (all-black images, weird text characters) are not applicable to this graph domain, and there are no explicit runtime sanity checks (e.g., NaN/Inf checks, empty graph filtering) that conclusively prove correctness purely from static inspection.
EVIDENCE: 
- DataModule and dataset choice: SmallGraphDataset loads standard PyTorch Geometric datasets (TUDataset, MoleculeNet) and a synthetic dataset, applying transforms and splits. It sets up stratified or KFold splits, returns PyG DataLoaders, and computes class ratios for weighting classification loss [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:277-334,399-477].
- Positional encodings preprocessing: The PaddedLaplacianPE transform safeguards eigenvector computation with a “safe k” and pads to a fixed dimension, indicating care to keep positional encodings well-formed even for small graphs [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:36-63,310-315]. RWPE and custom Laplacian PE are also implemented [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:184-213,136-181].
- Label and feature handling: OneHotDecoding converts one-hot labels to single class indices (to avoid inconsistent label shapes), and HIV-specific ConvertToCategorical maps categorical features to indices [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:256-274,91-100,317-323].
- Regression preprocessing: For regression datasets, y is standardized using StandardScaler fit on the training split and applied to val/test, a reasonable preprocessing step [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:452-474].
- Precomputation and collation: PrecomputeOneHopStructureOnly generates k-hop subgraph info per node and the custom_collate_fn reconstructs subgraph batches consistently, but these do not include explicit anomaly checks [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/kHopSubgraphTransform.py:10-38,76-128].

Additional information needed to conclude PASS/FAIL:
- Run-time logs or unit tests that load each dataset and validate properties (e.g., no NaN/Inf features or labels; no empty graphs; expected node/edge counts; positional encodings finite and correct shape).
- Sample batches printed or saved showing feature ranges/statistics post-transform, or assertions that catch degenerate cases.
- Since images/text are not involved, analogous graph-specific checks (e.g., no isolated graphs, reasonable degree distributions) would be required to confidently assert correctness.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains explicit Python loops for per-node operations where a batched/matrix alternative exists within the same codebase. Specifically, local ECT is computed with a Python for-loop across nodes instead of the available batched ECT approach using PyG Batch and ECTLayer.
EVIDENCE: 
- Non-vectorized local ECT computation loops over nodes and computes a k-hop subgraph and ECT per node, one by one: [LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/utility.py:172-203]. This includes computing the subgraph per node and invoking ECT inside the loop.
- A batched, more vectorized alternative is implemented elsewhere in the repo: building a Batch of neighborhoods and computing ECT over the batch (reducing Python-level overhead). See _compute_lect_batch_wise which constructs neighborhood batches and applies ECTLayer in batch: [LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/models/baseGraphModel.py:175-190]. This demonstrates that a matrix/batch approach is available and preferred over per-node loops.
- Additional instance of Python-level looping for feature mapping that could be vectorized with lookup tensors: ConvertToCategorical iterates over columns and rows with a Python loop/list comprehension for categorical mapping: [LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:91-100].

tests.description:
VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository sets seeds and uses deterministic evaluation dataloaders and eval() mode, but it does not enable PyTorch/PyG deterministic algorithms or provide a script to run evaluation multiple times on a fixed checkpoint. On GPU, some torch_geometric scatter/reduction kernels can be non-deterministic, which may affect outputs and thus accuracy. Without executing repeated evaluations, we cannot confirm that accuracy remains identical across runs.
EVIDENCE: 
- Seeds set at start of pipeline: ["/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:31-34"]
- Accelerator selection uses GPU if available (potential non-determinism in kernels): ["/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:43-49"]
- Validation/test DataLoaders have shuffle=False and fixed collation: ["/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:491-511"]
- Model set to eval() before testing: ["/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:195-196"], ["/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:212-214"]
- Only a single test is performed after training; no script repeats evaluation without retraining: ["/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:214-224"]
- No usage of deterministic controls like pl.seed_everything, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True), or cudnn.deterministic found in the codebase.

Additional information needed:
- A script or command that loads a fixed checkpoint and runs trainer.test multiple times in the same process (or separate processes) reporting test accuracy on each run, or logs from such runs showing identical accuracy values.
- Alternatively, explicit deterministic settings added to code (e.g., pl.Trainer(deterministic=True), torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True), torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True/benchmark=False) or forcing CPU evaluation to eliminate GPU kernel nondeterminism.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository consistently assigns a single accelerator (CPU/GPU), relies on PyTorch Lightning to move the LightningModule and batches to that device, and explicitly moves any newly constructed tensors/batches to the same device. No mixed CPU/GPU operations or implicit transfers are present in the training path, and there is no mixed-precision or dtype change logic; computations remain in float32 unless otherwise specified by default.
EVIDENCE: 
- Single-device selection and use:
  - Accelerator is chosen once and used everywhere, including ECT direction creation and Trainer setup [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:43-49, 73-78, 138-151].
- Model moved and data handled by Lightning:
  - The model is wrapped in a LightningModule and trained with pl.Trainer(accelerator=...), which automatically moves the module and batches to the chosen device [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:138-151].
- Explicit device alignment for constructed tensors/batches:
  - During local-ECT computation, the neighborhood batch is explicitly moved to the same device as x: neigh_batch = ... .to(x.device) [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/models/baseGraphModel.py:175-184].
  - In the ECT utility path, temporaries are constructed on x.device: scale and l_ects are created via .to(x.device) [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/utility.py:169-170].
  - For multi-layer ECT, new direction tensors are created on the same device as the initial directions (which were created using the chosen accelerator): device=self.ect_directions.device [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/models/gCNwithLECTallSteps.py:46-53].
- Registered buffers and metrics are attached to the module and will follow device moves:
  - Metrics and counters are registered as buffers; they will be on the same device as the module [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/models/modelWrapper.py:37-42].
- No implicit CPU↔GPU transfers or mixed dtypes:
  - The codebase lacks any use of autocast/AMP, half(), bfloat16/float16, or ad-hoc .cpu()/.cuda()/.to() device juggling in training; it sets matmul precision only (keeps fp32 compute) [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/experiments/train_gcn.py:28-29].
  - Labels/auxiliary tensors are created with explicit dtype (e.g., float32/long) and no mixed-precision logic is present [/workspace/LEAP_ Local ECT-Based Learnable Positional Encodings for Graphs [8XFPhByERc]/supplementary/leap/utils/dataset_loader.py:123, 272, 463-473].

REASON: The repository contains RL training code that acquires observations directly from Gymnasium Atari environments and performs basic preprocessing (frame skipping, resizing, normalization). However, there is no explicit data quality validation (e.g., checks for all-black frames), and without executing the code to inspect actual loaded observations, we cannot determine whether the data is “loaded and preprocessed correctly” per the test case examples.
EVIDENCE: 
- Environment construction and preprocessing use Gymnasium wrappers (seeded env, frame skip with max of last two frames, resize), but no quality checks for black images or anomalies were found: [/workspace/Mixture-of-World Models_ Scaling Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Modular Latent Dynamics [qUQARlAx5y]/supplementary/mow_atari_iclr/STORM-main/train.py:33-39], [/workspace/Mixture-of-World Models_ Scaling Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Modular Latent Dynamics [qUQARlAx5y]/supplementary/mow_atari_iclr/STORM-main/env_wrapper.py:48-76].
- Replay buffer stores uint8 observations from the env and normalizes them to [0,1] only at sample time, rearranging to channel-first; again, no data cleanliness checks (e.g., non-zero variance) are present: [/workspace/Mixture-of-World Models_ Scaling Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Modular Latent Dynamics [qUQARlAx5y]/supplementary/mow_atari_iclr/STORM-main/replay_buffer.py:18-22], [/workspace/Mixture-of-World Models_ Scaling Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Modular Latent Dynamics [qUQARlAx5y]/supplementary/mow_atari_iclr/STORM-main/replay_buffer.py:108-114], [/workspace/Mixture-of-World Models_ Scaling Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Modular Latent Dynamics [qUQARlAx5y]/supplementary/mow_atari_iclr/STORM-main/replay_buffer.py:117-133].
- The codebase does not handle text datasets or tabular data; only images from envs are used. Thus examples in the test such as “no text with weird characters” or “tables look correct” are not applicable based on static inspection.

Additional information needed to decide PASS/FAIL:
- Runtime evidence of loaded observations, e.g., sample batches of frames from the replay buffer with per-frame min/max/mean to confirm no all-black frames and reasonable pixel distributions.
- Screenshots or TensorBoard image/video logs produced during training to confirm visual integrity of observations.
- If any external trajectories are used (via load_trajectory), a quick validation of their contents (shape, dtype, non-constant images) would also be required.

tests.description:
VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository’s post-training script appears to set up validation correctly from the training split and uses the validation metric for checkpoint selection. However, it also optionally adds “extra validation” datasets whose provenance (test vs. validation splits) is imported from an external module not present in this repo. Without that external code or run configuration, it is not possible to definitively determine whether test data is being used during the training/validation loop.
EVIDENCE: 
- The fine-tuning script creates a validation set by splitting the training data and uses it for model selection (load_best_model_at_end), which is compliant: [/workspace/NIRVANA_ Structured Pruning Reimagined for Large Language Models Compression [55K9BdoOlo]/supplementary/NIRVANA/Llama/post_training.py:218-226], [/workspace/NIRVANA_ Structured Pruning Reimagined for Large Language Models Compression [55K9BdoOlo]/supplementary/NIRVANA/Llama/post_training.py:251-277].
- The same script can optionally add “extra validation datasets,” but the code imports the dataset getters from an external package not included here: [/workspace/NIRVANA_ Structured Pruning Reimagined for Large Language Models Compression [55K9BdoOlo]/supplementary/NIRVANA/Llama/post_training.py:237-249]. Specifically, it does:
  - from LLMPruner.datasets.ppl_dataset import get_wikitext2, get_ptb
  - _, test_data = get_wikitext2(...); val_data[extra_dataset] = test_data
  Because the external functions are not available in the repository, we cannot verify whether these return test or validation splits.
- Model selection is based on a validation metric only, via metric_for_best_model and load_best_model_at_end: [/workspace/NIRVANA_ Structured Pruning Reimagined for Large Language Models Compression [55K9BdoOlo]/supplementary/NIRVANA/Llama/post_training.py:251-277].

What’s needed to make a determination:
- The source code (or documentation) for LLMPruner.datasets.ppl_dataset.get_wikitext2 and get_ptb to verify which splits they return (test vs. validation).
- Confirmation (e.g., run configs or logs) whether the --extra_val_dataset option is actually used during training/model selection and whether metrics from those datasets influence checkpointing (metric_for_best_model).
- If the external getters do return test splits and those are included in eval_dataset during training, that would constitute leakage from test into validation, causing a FAIL under the test case conditions. Otherwise, if they return validation-only splits, the repository would PASS.

REASON: The code does not keep the model and inputs consistently on a single device and shows inconsistent dtype policy. REASON: The repository delegates most reported benchmark metrics to EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness, but the task configuration files (YAMLs) that define the exact dataset split(s) and metric selections per task are not present in this copy of the repo. - In MS-ResNet, the test DataLoader uses a DistributedSampler without specifying shuffle (default True) when a sampler is provided, leading to shuffled test data. VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository’s evaluation relies on text generation from LLMs where determinism depends on runtime generation settings (e.g., whether sampling is enabled) and potential use of an LLM-as-judge. From static code inspection, these settings are not consistently or explicitly fixed to deterministic values across all entry points. Without executing the evaluation or knowing the default generation_config.do_sample for the exact model/version used in the authors’ environment, we cannot conclusively determine if accuracy remains identical across repeated runs.
EVIDENCE: 
- Generation evaluation notebook loads Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and generates answers with a very small temperature (1e-10), but does not explicitly set do_sample False. Determinism hinges on whether sampling is enabled by default in the model’s generation config, which is not shown here. Torch/NumPy seeds are not set (only Python’s random.seed is set for unrelated selection): [supplementary/PreferenceOptimization/generation_eval.ipynb:223-235], [supplementary/PreferenceOptimization/generation_eval.ipynb:188-214], [supplementary/PreferenceOptimization/generation_eval.ipynb:431-435].
- The same notebook defines an LLM-as-judge path using OpenAI Chat Completions, which is non-deterministic if used (no temperature/seed control): [supplementary/PreferenceOptimization/generation_eval.ipynb:260-263] and usage defined in [supplementary/PreferenceOptimization/generation_eval.ipynb:475-493]. It’s unclear from the repository whether this path is used in reported evaluations.
- The reformulation inference script used to create query files for retrieval evaluation calls model.generate with temperature/top_p but without explicitly disabling sampling. Whether this is deterministic depends on the model’s default generation_config; there is no explicit do_sample=False nor seeding: [supplementary/CQR/reformulate_query.py:397-404], [supplementary/CQR/reformulate_query.py:421-428], [supplementary/CQR/reformulate_query.py:470-472].
- Retrieval evaluation (BM25/dense) itself is deterministic given fixed queries, but determinism would be affected if the upstream generated queries are non-deterministic.

Additional information needed to decide PASS/FAIL:
- The exact generation_config used at evaluation time for the LLMs (specifically whether do_sample is False). A copy of model.generation_config or the printed value of model.generation_config.do_sample during evaluation would suffice.
- Confirmation whether the LLM-as-judge evaluation (llm_eval) is used for accuracy reporting. If it is used, determinism is unlikely without a fixed, deterministic judging process.
- Two successive evaluation run logs (including generated predictions and final accuracy metrics) using the same inputs and environment to verify whether the outputs and accuracy are identical across runs.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository’s evaluation code uses vectorized/matrix operations where appropriate (e.g., batched CLIP similarity via tensor matmul and diagonal extraction, NumPy mean/covariance for FID) and only uses explicit loops for tasks that are inherently iterative (I/O, dataset iteration, OCR word matching). I found no evidence of elementwise numeric computation implemented with Python loops where equivalent matrix operations should have been used.
EVIDENCE: 
- CLIP scoring performs batched feature extraction and vectorized similarity via matrix multiplication and diagonal extraction, not per-sample loops: [(image_features @ text_features.T).diagonal()] [/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_clip_score.py:95-99]. It only loops to construct batches and map indices back to scores, which are I/O/control tasks: [/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_clip_score.py:61-75,100-104].
- FID computation uses vectorized NumPy operations for statistics (mean, covariance) and scipy sqrtm; loops are solely over DataLoader batches (model inference/I-O) rather than elementwise numeric loops: [/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_fid.py:69-79,102-115].
- OCR evaluation relies on fuzzy string matching that is not amenable to vectorized matrix ops (fuzz.ratio across variable-length word lists). The nested loops iterate over words for matching; no numeric tensor computations are implemented via Python loops: [/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_ocr.py:110-116].
- Repository contains only these Python evaluation scripts; no other computational modules were found that could hide vectorizable loops. The Python sources examined were the entire set under supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation: cal_clip_score.py, cal_fid.py, cal_ocr.py, cal_ocr_cer.py, eval_script.py.

VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The code clearly implements the claimed metric definitions (CLIP-ViT-B/32 similarity; OCR metrics with an 80% fuzzy match threshold; CER), but it is unclear whether the reported results were computed on the correct split. The evaluation script loads the Hugging Face dataset with split="train", while the paper describes TextAtlasEval as a test set. Without access to the Hugging Face dataset’s split definitions or explicit documentation clarifying that “train” corresponds to the intended evaluation/test split, we cannot determine if the reported metrics use the correct splits.
EVIDENCE:
- Paper claims TextAtlasEval is a test set, and defines metrics: CLIP-ViT-B/32 similarity; OCR word-level Accuracy, F1, and CER with 80% fuzzy tolerance:
  - “we curate 4,000 human-improved test cases (TextAtlasEval)…” [/evidence/artifacts/TextAtlas5M_paper.txt:24-35]
  - “For evaluation, we compute image-text similarity using CLIP-ViT-B/32… For OCR-based metrics… We report word-level accuracy, F1 score, and character error rate (CER), allowing up to 80% mismatch tolerance in word-level evaluation.” [/evidence/artifacts/TextAtlas5M_paper.txt:652-658]
- Evaluation script loads split="train" from the evaluation dataset “CSU-JPG/TextAtlasEval” (dataset_type chosen among “styledtextsynth”, “textvisionblend”, “textsceneshq”), with no documentation stating this is the test/eval split:
  - [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/eval_script.py:18-27]
- CLIP score implementation matches the claimed CLIP-ViT-B/32 cosine similarity (normalized features, averaged across samples):
  - Model: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 (ViT-B/32) [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_clip_score.py:10-13]
  - Cosine similarity of normalized image/text features [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_clip_score.py:52-57]
  - Average over dataset [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_clip_score.py:130-136]
- OCR metrics use PaddleOCR and fuzzy word-level matching with threshold=80 by default; overall Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 are computed from global counts (micro-averaged), while CER is averaged per sample (macro):
  - Fuzzy threshold default 80, PaddleOCR usage [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_ocr.py:70-76]
  - Fuzzy match with fuzz.ratio >= threshold [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_ocr.py:109-116]
  - Overall metrics aggregated via total correct/predicted/ground-truth words (micro) [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_ocr.py:185-200]
  - CER computed per entry with Levenshtein distance and averaged across entries (macro) [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/cal_ocr_cer.py:9-33, 72-75]
- Evaluation README shows how to run evaluations but does not specify split names or clarify that “train” is the eval/test split:
  - [/workspace/TextAtlas5M_ A Large-Scale Dataset for Long and Structured Text Image Generation [8yJyEKHkB8]/supplementary/EvalCode/evaluation/README.md:22-33, 36-55]

- If different splits exist (train/val/test), explicit documentation or code referencing which split(s) were used to produce the reported results in the tables.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The evaluation pipeline includes uncontrolled stochasticity in model generation that can change results across runs. In particular, Anthropic (Claude) API calls do not use any seed and default to nonzero temperature, and local model server selection uses Python’s random without a fixed seed. Therefore, running the evaluation multiple times (without retraining) can yield different outputs and thus different accuracy/metrics.
EVIDENCE:
- Anthropic (Claude) API path uses temperature and no seed, making outputs nondeterministic by default: [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/agents/role_client.py:181-189] and [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/agents/role_client.py:192-205].
- The data model explicitly notes that model_seed is not used for Anthropic models: [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/types.py:30-33].

- While OpenAI/vLLM code paths pass a seed (which can make those specific calls deterministic), this is not universally enforced across all supported models, so the evaluation as a whole is not guaranteed to be deterministic: OpenAI/gpt path with seed [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/agents/role_client.py:213-220] and vLLM path with seed [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/agents/role_client.py:231-238].

tests.description:
VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repo defines and computes several metrics (counts of end conditions, average turns, and derived rates), but it’s not possible to verify that the reported metrics use the exact definitions claimed and the correct splits without the actual experiment configs and outputs. In particular, the analysis scripts hardcode a denominator of 32 games, and “both” end conditions are included in both miscommunication and interception tallies, which may or may not match the textual definitions in the paper. The repository also references missing configuration files for reproducing paper results, leaving ambiguity about the splits and settings used.
EVIDENCE: 
- End condition counting in core game loop shows four outcomes and how they are tallied:
  - End-condition updates when a game finishes, incrementing miscomm, intercept, both, or survived (and computing turns):
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/runner.py:338-352]
  - Initialization of end condition dictionary and subsequent aggregation to stats:
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/runner.py:72-85]
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/src/runner.py:420-431]
- Analysis script for heatmaps derives proportions by dividing counts by a hardcoded 32, and includes “both” cases in totals:
  - Competitive intercepts per game calculated as (intercepts + both) / 32:
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/analysis/comp_cross_4heatmaps.py:114-125]
  - Cross-play miscommunications per game calculated as (miscomms + both) / 32:
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/analysis/comp_cross_4heatmaps.py:176-186]
- Human replay rates are defined as token counts divided by 2 and episodes; this matches the game’s 2-token rule but relies on how totals are tallied (and does not clarify treatment of “both”):
  - Rate formulae: interception_rate = total_interceptions / 2 / total_episodes, and similar for miscommunication:
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/analysis/extract_human_stats.py:9-17]
- The paper describes figures such as “Percentage of games ending in miscommunications” and “proportion of games ending in an intercept,” but does not clarify treatment of “both” in those percentages:
  - Figure caption language:
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/paper.txt:296-304]
- The README claims reproducibility configs under config/paper, but no config directory exists in the repo, making it impossible to verify the exact splits/settings used for reported results:
  - “Reproducing results” reference:
    [/workspace/The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind [epfwDqw7wn]/supplementary/README.md:139-141]

Additional information needed to make a determination:
- The exact configuration files used to generate the reported metrics (e.g., the missing config/paper), including the number of episodes per combination (to confirm the hardcoded 32 denominator).
- An explicit definition for how “both” end conditions are handled when computing “percentage of games ending in miscommunication” and “percentage of games ending in an intercept.”
- The actual experiment outputs (CSV summaries or logs) used to produce figures/tables in the paper, to verify that the analysis scripts match the claimed metric definitions and splits.

  [/workspace/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/evaluate_e.py:111-121]
- UNKE and MQuake/AKEW evaluation helpers call the model directly without ensuring eval mode (only torch.no_grad is used), so dropout remains active:
  - AKEW neighborhood evaluation uses model(**prompts_inp) directly:
    [/workspace/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/py/eval_utils_akew.py:67-71]
  - MQuake batch prediction uses model(**prompt_tok) directly:
    [/workspace/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/py/eval_utils_mquake.py:110-117]
- MMLU evaluation uses greedy decoding (do_sample=False) but still depends on model.forward; without model.eval(), dropout can introduce nondeterminism in predicted answers and thus accuracy metrics:

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains multiple instances of explicit Python loops and control flow used to perform operations that could be implemented more efficiently with vectorized/matrix operations in PyTorch. These patterns appear in core numeric code paths (e.g., computing grouped means, sliding-window KL over sequences, and token-level probability aggregation), where vectorized torch operations (reshape, mean over dimensions, gather, unfold/as_strided, and masked reductions) would eliminate Python loops.
EVIDENCE: 
- Grouped mean computation implemented with nested loops rather than vectorized reduction:
  [Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/baselines/alphaEdit/compute_ks.py:39-50] — Constructs cumulative group boundaries and then loops over ranges to compute means. This can be vectorized by reshaping layer_ks to (num_requests, context_len, d) and using torch.mean across grouped slices without Python loops.
- Sliding-window KL computation iterates over batch and constructs windows with Python comprehensions instead of tensor operations:
  [Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/PTE/ours_plug.py:49-69] and [Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/PTE/ours_plug.py:148-167] — Loops over bs and uses list comprehensions to build stacked windows. This could be replaced with tensor ops such as torch.nn.functional.unfold/as_strided over the sequence dimension or batched slicing, avoiding Python-level loops.
- Token-level probability aggregation and accuracy checks done with nested Python loops instead of batched gather and reductions:
  [Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/py/eval_utils_akew.py:183-205] — Iterates over sequence positions to sum negative log-probs and check argmax per token. This can be vectorized with torch.gather on precomputed token indices and mask-based reductions.
- Additional loop-based per-sample target mask construction in training objective:
  [Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/baselines/alphaEdit/compute_z.py:63-66] — Builds rewriting_targets with a for-loop based on attention mask lengths; can be vectorized using index computations and scatter/gather ops.

These examples show reliance on explicit loops where vectorized tensor operations would be more efficient, thus failing the stated test condition.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository does not consistently enforce a single-device policy or a coherent dtype policy. The model is instantiated with device_map='auto' (which can shard layers across devices and even offload to CPU), while many downstream utilities hardcode .to("cuda") for inputs, intermediate tensors, and weight restoration. This mixture can trigger implicit device transfers and mismatches. Additionally, dtype usage is ad hoc: some computations upcast to float64 and later cast back to float32, but there is no consistent, global dtype policy (e.g., fp32 or bf16) applied throughout the code.

REASON: The repo contains code that computes multiple reported metrics (ROUGE-L F1, BERTScore, GLUE-task metrics, and an MMLU proxy). Some implementations diverge from typical/standard definitions (e.g., MMLU uses a weighted F1 proxy instead of accuracy; GLUE tasks use weighted F1 and a custom few-shot/test split on a balanced subset of the validation set), but the paper does not state precise metric definitions or splits for those figures. Without the exact reporting details (which split, averaging scheme, and which metrics for each task) it’s not possible to determine if the reported metrics used the correct split(s) and exact definitions claimed.
EVIDENCE:
- Paper claims for AKEW/UnKEBench metrics (BERTScore and ROUGE-L F1): The PDF states they use BERTScore (cosine similarity of contextual embeddings) and ROUGE-L precision/recall with F1 reported. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/3922_Towards_Understanding_the.pdf:360-372]
- Code for AKEW/UNKE summarization computes macro-averaged per-sample ROUGE-L Precision/Recall/F1 via python-rouge and BERTScore via SentenceTransformer cosine, then scales by 100, which is consistent with those claims but not sufficient to prove that these are the exact settings used for the reported tables/figures: [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/summarize_e.py:24-26,55-75,103-110]; [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/summarize_base.py:24-26,55-76,105-110]
- GLUE evaluation uses custom subsets and nonstandard metrics:
  - Subset creation builds pickled subsets from GLUE validation (e.g., sst2.pkl), balancing classes with alternating rows; not standard GLUE splits. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/dataset/create_glue_subset.py:34-62]
  - The few-shot/test split for GLUE loaders uses the first 10 examples as few-shots (FEW_SHOT_TEST_SPLIT=10), remaining examples for testing; supports optional begin_id windowing. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/useful_functions.py:22-35]
  - Task evaluators compute weighted F1 and MCC, and additionally a token-probability-based variant f1_new; these differ from standard GLUE metrics (e.g., SST-2 accuracy, CoLA MCC). Examples: SST weighted F1 and f1_new [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/sst_eval.py:166-187]; MRPC weighted F1 and f1_new [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/mrpc_eval.py:206-240]; CoLA weighted F1 and f1_new [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/cola_eval.py:190-220]; RTE weighted F1/f1_new [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/rte_eval.py:207-240]; NLI weighted F1/f1_new [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/nli_eval.py:214-260].
  - The GLUE wrapper simply collects these task metrics; it does not define a standard GLUE score. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/glue_eval.py:49-97]
  - The paper references “Performance on GLUE” in Figure 8 but does not specify which metrics/averaging/splits were used, making it impossible to confirm consistency with the code’s custom evaluations. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/3922_Towards_Understanding_the.pdf:1560-1605,1641-1660]
- MMLU evaluation: The evaluation code defines MMLU as a multiple-choice task but computes a weighted F1 (and f1_new) rather than accuracy, and the AKEW/UNKE evaluation uses result_dict['f1_new'] as an MMLU result. This is a nonstandard definition; the paper does not state any MMLU metric definition. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/mmlu_eval.py:216-220]; [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/glue_eval/mmlu_eval_each.py:217-233]; [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/py/eval_utils_akew.py:48-56]
- Pipeline: AKEW/UNKE run metrics saved and later summarized include ‘mmlu_result’ values populated from the MMLU f1_new, and generation_result used for ROUGE/BERTScore. [/Towards Understanding the Effect of NTP Paradigm in Unstructured Knowledge Editing [8TkNRNboyg]/supplementary/EvEdit/experiments/evaluate_e.py:215-223]

Additional information required to determine PASS/FAIL:
- Exact metric definitions used for each reported result (especially the GLUE and MMLU figures): which tasks, which metric per task (e.g., SST-2 accuracy vs weighted F1), averaging (micro/macro/weighted), and whether the “f1_new” variant was used in place of standard metrics.
- Exact dataset splits used for each reported result:
  - For GLUE: which split (train/dev/test), whether a custom balanced subset was used, the few-shot/test partition details (e.g., FEW_SHOT_TEST_SPLIT=10), and the evaluation set size.
  - For MMLU: which dataset split/subset was used and whether accuracy or F1 was reported.
- Confirmation that AKEW/UnKEBench reported ROUGE-L F1 and BERTScore were computed per-sample then macro-averaged and scaled as in summarize_e, and which embeddings backbone was used for BERTScore (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2).

While the paper also mentions evaluation on VBench prompts, the repository does not include code or a prompt list to verify splits; however, the clear mismatch in the NoRepeat metric definition alone suffices to fail this test.

They also state they report the mean NoRepeat Score across videos [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/5061_UltraViCo_Breaking_Extrap.pdf:1059-1061].
- The tables present NoRepeat with an upward arrow (↑), implying higher is better (i.e., less repetition), which is consistent with a non-repetition ratio, not a repetition ratio [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/5061_UltraViCo_Breaking_Extrap.pdf:382-391], [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/5061_UltraViCo_Breaking_Extrap.pdf:1110-1124].
- Provided implementation code labeled “no_repeat_score.py” shows:
  • Static-video filtering using 8 uniformly sampled frames and an L2 threshold of 55 [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/supplementary/code/no_repeat_score/no_repeat_score.py:15-25], [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/supplementary/code/no_repeat_score/no_repeat_score.py:7].
  • Repetition detection by finding a candidate offset around a provided theoretical period [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/supplementary/code/no_repeat_score/no_repeat_score.py:27-39].
  • Crucially, the score returned is (offset + sum(differences)) / T, where ‘differences’ increments when frames are NOT similar (L2 >= THRESHOLD), i.e., counts non-repeated frames. This computes a non-repetition ratio, not the “ratio of repeated frames” as claimed [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/supplementary/code/no_repeat_score/no_repeat_score.py:46-57], [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/supplementary/code/no_repeat_score/no_repeat_score.py:57].
- Evaluation setup claims: “we use 100 prompts sampled from VBench … except for HunyuanVideo at 4×, where we use 25 prompts” [/workspace/UltraViCo_ Breaking Extrapolation Limits in Video Diffusion Transformers [fLLCmC53u9]/5061_UltraViCo_Breaking_Extrap.pdf:403-406]. The repo does not include code or a definitive prompt list for the evaluation split to verify this, but the definitional mismatch above is already sufficient for FAIL.

REASON: The repository’s data loader and preprocessing logic contain inconsistencies and omissions that indicate data will not be loaded and preprocessed correctly. Specifically, .npy files are transposed in a way that conflicts with the expected dataset shape, the DataModule assumes an axis order it does not ensure, the Dataset strictly requires 3D inputs without the DataModule guaranteeing that shape, and the DataModule claims to “slice” sequences but includes no slicing implementation.
EVIDENCE: 
- TSGDataset requires each dataset to be 3D; otherwise it asserts. However, the DataModule does not ensure this when loading 2D arrays, and claims to perform slicing without implementing it:
  - 3D requirement in dataset: [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/ldm/data/tsg_dataset.py:11-15]
  - DataModule claims “Slicing is also done with this module” but the split function only shuffles/splits without any slicing: [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/ldm/data/tsg_dataset.py:61-66], [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/ldm/data/tsg_dataset.py:119-128]
  - __getitem__ expects 3D arrays and indexes [:, :, 0], which will fail if the input remained 2D: [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/ldm/data/tsg_dataset.py:45-57]
- The loader for .npy files unconditionally transposes the loaded array, assuming an original shape of (N, T). This is incompatible with the preprocessed datasets used in this project (which are (n, t, c)), and will produce incorrect axis ordering for 3D data:
  - .npy loader transposes arrays: [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/ldm/data/tsg_dataset.py:231-238]
  - The DataModule then treats 3D input as (n, t, c) and rearranges as ‘n t c -> (n c) t 1’, which is wrong if .npy files were already transposed to (c, t, n): [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/ldm/data/tsg_dataset.py:96-105]
- The repo’s own utilities indicate the expected .npy shape is (n, t, c) for the preprocessed TimeDP datasets, and they do not transpose on load, further highlighting the inconsistency:
  - Expected shape (n, t, c) for preprocessed .npy and optional univariate rearrangement: [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/utils/data_utils.py:33-38]
- The Readme instructs using the preprocessed TimeDP datasets, which are provided as .npy files, aligning with the above expected shape and amplifying the mismatch with the .npy loader’s transpose: [/workspace/Winformer_ Transcending pairwise similarity for time-series generation [DY6dnkRKo7]/supplementary/codes/Readme.md:18-26]

These issues demonstrate that the data is not guaranteed to be loaded and preprocessed correctly under the repo’s intended usage (TimeDP .npy datasets), thus failing the test.
